# Brief: settle the noise complaint from the offices above the despatch bay

The tenants on the second floor have complained three times since June and the
last letter came from their solicitor. This is now a landlord problem with a
deadline attached, and the deadline is the lease review in November.

## What we know

The complaint is about noise between 0530 and 0730, which is when despatch runs
its first wave. Nobody upstairs disputes that a despatch bay makes noise; what
they object to is a specific intermittent sound they describe as a "grinding
shriek" lasting a few seconds, several times an hour.

Our own maintenance log for the same period records nothing unusual. The
conveyor was serviced in April, the sprocket on the incline drive was replaced
at the same time, and the service sheet is signed and unremarkable. Facilities'
position is that the equipment is within spec and the tenants moved into a
building with a despatch bay in it.

I do not think that position survives a solicitor's letter, and I do not think
it is a good position anyway. A sound somebody can pick out of the background
and describe consistently is a sound with a source, and we should find it.

## What I want you to do

This is a measurement job first and a negotiation second, and the order matters
because we have nothing to negotiate with until we have numbers.

- Get a proper acoustic measurement, in the offices rather than in the bay, over
  at least a full working week including one weekend for a baseline. Hire the
  instrument and hire somebody who has used one before; a phone app will be
  discredited in about four seconds by anybody they bring.
- Correlate the peaks against the despatch schedule and against what the
  building management system logs — doors, ventilation, the goods lift.
- Interview two of the complainants directly. What they can tell you that an
  instrument cannot is whether the sound has changed character over time, which
  is the single most useful piece of information for finding a mechanical
  source.

## Constraints

- Do not stop despatch to test. The first wave is what makes the day work and a
  morning lost costs more than the whole investigation.
- Do not commit us to remediation in any conversation with the tenants until we
  know what is making the noise. An offer made before the cause is known becomes
  the floor for every negotiation afterwards.
- Anything structural is out of scope this year. If the answer is that the slab
  transmits and needs isolating, that is a capital conversation and a different
  brief.

## What good looks like

A short written finding that says what the sound is, when it happens, how loud
it is where they sit, and what it would cost to reduce. If the honest answer is
that the noise is within the limits the lease permits and the tenants simply do
not like it, say that too, with the numbers — but say it after measuring rather
than before.

## Reporting

Come to me before you talk to the tenants' solicitor, always. And keep facilities
in the loop as you go rather than presenting to them at the end; they have been
doing this building for eleven years and the fastest route to the source is
probably a conversation with the person who has heard it before.

## One more thing

The despatch supervisor has been told twice that the complaint is "being looked
at" and has heard nothing since. He is the person most likely to know what the
sound is and he currently has no reason to help. Go and talk to him first, tell
him what you are actually doing, and ask him what he thinks it is. If his answer
turns out to be right — which in my experience it usually is — say so in the
finding with his name on it.

## Budget

The measurement is a few thousand pounds and I have signed it off already. Do
not spend beyond that without asking; if the answer turns out to need a longer
survey, come back with what the first week showed and I will find the rest.
